etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
paragraphs: From Middle English bageard (“marked by a badge”), from bage (“badge”), referring to the animal's badge-like white blaze, equivalent to badge +‎ -ard. Displaced earlier brock, from Old English brocc, ultimately from Proto-Celtic *brokkos. The unattested, native word may be Old English *þæx, *þæxe; from Proto-West Germanic *þahs; from Proto-Germanic *þahsuz.
senses: Any member of species of the genera Meles, Arctonyx, Mellivora or Taxidea, of mammals.
(transitive) To pester; to annoy persistently; to press.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
paragraphs: Unknown Possibly from bagger. "Baggier" is cited by the OED in 1467-8.
senses: (obsolete) An itinerant licensed dealer in commodities used for food; a hawker or huckster; especially one who bought grain in one place and sold it in another.
